orders.explanation: Transcript 2 implements the RFC 7231 rule correctly by computing the two-digit year within the *current century* and rolling it back one century only if it lands more than 50 years in the future. Transcript 1’s final logic hard-codes a 1900/2000 choice based on `current_year % 100`, which breaks for years outside the 2000–2099 range (e.g., it would misinterpret years when the current year is 1999 or 2105). Transcript 2 is therefore both more standards-correct and more robust across time.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it implements the RFC 7231 rule using a true “current century + two-digit year, then roll back a century if >50 years in the future” approach, which remains correct even near century boundaries (e.g., year 2098 interpreting “01” as 2101). Transcript 2’s final formula (`year += 2000 if year - current_year % 100 <= 50 else 1900`) works for many present-day cases but breaks around century transitions because it never considers the current century and thus can map future-near years incorrectly. While Transcript 2 shows iterative debugging and runs Django’s test runner, the final algorithm is less robust and standards-faithful than Transcript 1’s.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger debugging and validation skills: it reproduces the issue end-to-end with a minimal Sphinx project, traces the root cause through Sphinx and docutils internals (including why leading spaces in option values are lost), finds the relevant upstream fix/commit, implements the correct filter reordering, and adds a targeted regression test while running the full relevant test suite. Transcript 2 applies essentially the same code change but with less rigorous investigation, no new regression test, and weaker tooling/patch workflow (attempting a nonexistent `applypatch`). Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper understanding and more robust engineering practice.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it performs deeper root-cause analysis (confirming the whitespace loss originates in docutils option parsing), validates behavior with a minimal Sphinx project, and triangulates the correct fix by locating the upstream commit that already addressed the issue. It also adds a targeted regression test and runs the relevant test suite to ensure the fix is both correct and durable. Transcript 1 applies the same core fix and runs tests, but does less investigation and omits adding a regression test.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it diagnoses and fixes the full set of NumPy 2.x removals systematically across both Python and Cython sources (including correct dtype replacements like `np.int_`, `np.float64`, `np.bool_`, `np.complex128`), then rebuilds and verifies the compiled extensions. It also catches and resolves additional real-world breakages (Python 3.13 `fractions.gcd` removal and `planarity` 1.0 attribute renames) in a robust, version-tolerant way, and validates both in-tree and globally installed behavior with tests and explicit `.so` provenance checks. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working state but is more ad hoc (multiple incomplete patches, reliance on `float/int` in places where NumPy dtypes are more appropriate, and less clean handling of the `planarity` change), indicating weaker debugging and packaging rigor.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it systematically audits and fixes the full set of NumPy 2.x deprecations (including `np.bool`, which Transcript 1 appears to miss), verifies compilation, verifies runtime behavior from outside the source tree (ensuring the global install is used), and cleanly resolves the `planarity` attribute rename with a minimal normalization layer. Transcript 1 does eventually reach a working state, but it relies on ad‑hoc patching (including partial greps and manual fixes after failed patch tooling) and shows more trial-and-error and less comprehensive coverage of compatibility surface area.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end capability: it systematically overcame Cloudflare by switching to the official FTP service, identified and fetched the correct combination of archives (source + docs/includes needed for `+L`), built using the intended UNIX makefiles, and then debugged two subtle correctness issues (linker symbol case mismatch and non-deterministic nonzero exit status from `void main`) to ensure the provided sanity-check command exits cleanly. Transcript 2 is resourceful in bootstrapping a musl toolchain when no compiler is present, but it takes a riskier path (musl static build and manual include-tree flattening) and doesn’t demonstrate the same depth of debugging/robustness around runtime/exit-code correctness.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger problem-solving under tighter constraints: it recognizes the environment has neither `make` nor any C compiler, then successfully bootstraps a standalone musl GCC toolchain and produces a working static binary (also handling the missing runtime loader issue). It also finds a viable mirror (ftp.icm.edu.pl) and adapts the documentation include path to match the required `+L` directory. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds, but spends significant effort on dead-end HTTP/Wayback/SourceForge approaches and requires source/config edits to fix build/exit-code issues in a more conventional environment after installing build tools via apt.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it performs a complete, disciplined debugging loop: reproduces the segfault deterministically, obtains a gdb backtrace, pinpoints the precise invariant violation by comparing traversal patterns across multiple functions, applies a minimal correct fix, and then verifies it with a full rebuild and a clean run of the required basic testsuite. Transcript 2 finds the same bug, but its workflow is less reliable (failed patch tooling, ad‑hoc edit), does not successfully run the requested testsuite, and leaves verification incomplete.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it systematically reproduces the segfault, obtains a precise backtrace with gdb to confirm heap corruption during marking, and then validates the suspected invariant by comparing `pool_sweep` against other correct pool traversal functions in the same file. It applies the minimal correct fix, completes a full rebuild successfully, and crucially runs the requested basic testsuite target to completion with a clean summary. Transcript 1 finds the same underlying bug, but fails to apply the patch cleanly with proper tooling, does not complete a full bootstrap build in the session, and cannot run the required testsuite target to verify correctness.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it diagnoses and fixes the mteb `encode()` API requirements correctly (task_name must correspond to an actual MTEB task), inspects the wrapper/prompt logic to choose an appropriate task (`T2Retrieval`) and prompt usage, and validates the final answer by printing the full ranking and verifying `/app/result.txt`. It also performs a robustness check (with/without query prompt) and explicitly justifies why the prompted retrieval setup is the faithful interpretation. Transcript 2 eventually runs, but it largely relies on trial-and-error, provides no ranking/verification of the selected line’s content, and leaves more ambiguity about correctness.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only fixes the `mteb`-specific API requirements (`task_name`, `PromptType`) but also surfaces the full similarity ranking, writes the exact 5th-ranked line, and verifies the written output. It additionally performs a robustness check (with/without query prompt) and justifies why the prompted retrieval setup is the appropriate interpretation for bge retrieval, demonstrating stronger debugging discipline and task understanding. Transcript 1 eventually runs without error, but it never reveals the selected line, provides no ranking evidence, and appears to have questionable indexing/selection (reporting `idx_5th = 1`) without validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger problem-solving: it precisely identifies the specific overfull hbox sources from the log, then uses a systematic automated search/hill-climbing approach to find a minimal set of synonym substitutions that eliminates all warnings, followed by careful verification that only allowed edits were made and that outputs are clean. Transcript 2 eventually fixes the warnings but does so with a large number of broad, somewhat careless replacements (including awkward phrasing and an attempted use of missing tools), indicating less control and optimization.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it builds an automated optimization loop that compiles candidates in parallel, directly minimizes total overfull “pt too wide,” and converges to a *minimal* set of synonym swaps that eliminates all warnings. It also verifies constraints (no changes to `main.tex`/`synonyms.txt`), confirms zero overfulls via log grepping, and carefully handles file fidelity (e.g., newline preservation) despite tooling limitations (no python3, no xxd). Transcript 1 reaches a clean compile but does so with many unnecessary, sometimes awkward semantic-altering edits and several manual iterations, indicating weaker control and optimization.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a more systematic, targeted forensic workflow: it searches within /app, quickly homes in on the embedded ZIP signatures, carves the relevant region with correct offsets, and reconstructs the password with fewer unnecessary detours. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but wastes substantial time on broad root scans/timeouts and incorrect hypotheses (e.g., treating the blob as tar), indicating weaker efficiency and investigative discipline.

Transcript 1 is the more capable model because it follows a tighter, more forensic-relevant plan and converges quickly once it detects the embedded ZIP structures, adapting smoothly to missing tooling (no git, no python, no xxd/hexdump) by using byte-offset grep, dd carving, and strings. Transcript 2 eventually reconstructs and validates the password, but wastes time on broad, slow system-wide searches (including a timeout), makes an incorrect “tar archive” hypothesis, and shows less efficient investigative focus before reaching the same ZIP-based conclusion.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it delivers a clean, complete implementation and explicitly validates correctness with multi-process tests across world sizes, including checking sharding and matching reference outputs and gradients. It also implements autograd-safe collective ops for both all-gather and all-reduce semantics, ensuring gradient behavior is correct rather than relying on side effects. Transcript 2 has a reasonable design (and even handles uneven splits), but the execution is much less reliable—multiple failed file-write attempts and no demonstrated verification of gradients or forward correctness.

Transcript 1 shows a more sophisticated and generally correct tensor-parallel implementation: it shards with a rank-aware partition function that supports uneven splits and implements an autograd-safe all_gather+concat that pads/trim shards so communication works even when shard sizes differ. It also safely handles the case where `torch.distributed` is not initialized, which can matter in some test harnesses. Transcript 2 is cleaner and well-tested but relies on `torch.chunk` plus `dist.all_gather` with `empty_like(x)`, which will break when shard sizes differ across ranks (a common edge case), indicating a less robust understanding of distributed collective shape constraints.
